lmsArticle.title: How to serve data at lightning speed | Caching Strategies (Redis/Memcached)
lmsArticle.subtitle: Unlock blazing-fast data delivery and drastically reduce database load with advanced caching strategies using Redis and Memcached.
lmsArticle.excerpt: Master caching to accelerate data access, improve system responsiveness, and scale efficiently.
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context

Caching accelerates application performance by storing frequently accessed data in fast, in-memory key-value stores like Redis or Memcached. Selecting the correct caching strategy—such as Cache-Aside, Write-Through, or Write-Behind—determines how data consistency is maintained between the cache and the primary database.



```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "TLDR:** Caching accelerates application performa…

This walkthrough focuses on **The Performance Problem: Database Bottlenecks**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- In modern web development, database access is often the primary bottleneck.
- Relational databases (like PostgreSQL or MySQL) store data on disk.
- When a client requests a resource, the application server must execute a SQL query, parse the request, scan table indexes, read disk blocks into memory, perform joins, and return the result.

**Concepts in play:** caching, consistency-replication, database-indexing, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection

## Stage 1 — Caching Patterns

- The flow of data between the application, the cache, and the database is governed by specific caching patterns.
- Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) This is the most common caching pattern.
- The application is responsible for managing both the cache and the database.
- - Read Flow: The application checks the cache.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "Caching Patterns - Storage Topology",
  "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.",
  "view": "data-flow",
  "pattern": "cache-aside",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": [
    { "id": "compute", "label": "Application Workers", "tone": "blue" },
    { "id": "cache-tier", "label": "Volatile Memory Tier", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "storage-tier", "label": "Persistent Disk Tier", "tone": "green" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "worker", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Worker Process", "group": "compute" },
    { "id": "mem", "component": "redis", "label": "In-Memory Cache", "group": "cache-tier", "badge": "Hot Keys" },
    { "id": "primary", "component": "postgres", "label": "Primary Database", "group": "storage-tier", "badge": "Write Master" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "worker", "to": "mem", "kind": "read", "label": "Fast Read" },
    { "from": "worker", "to": "primary", "kind": "write", "label": "Transactional Commit" }
  ],
  "takeaway": {
    "title": "Storage Access Pattern",
    "body": "In-memory caching handles high-frequency read spikes, reserving disk transactions strictly for state modifications."
  }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** - Read Flow: The application checks the cache.

## Stage 2 — Eviction Policies and TTL

- Memory (RAM) is expensive and limited.
- A cache cannot grow indefinitely.
- To manage memory constraints, caches use two mechanisms: Time-To-Live (TTL) and Eviction Policies .
- Time-To-Live (TTL) Every cached key should be assigned an expiration timer (TTL).

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Time-To-Live (TTL) Every cached key should be assigned an expiration timer (TTL).

## Stage 3 — Caching Gotchas and Mitigation

- Cache Avalanche - The Problem: A large number of cached keys expire at the exact same time, or the cache server crashes.
- This causes all client traffic to hit the database simultaneously, causing a database crash.
- - Mitigation: Add a random jitter (e.g., adding a random offset of 1 to 5 minutes) to the TTL of every key, spreading expiration events evenly over time.
- Cache Penetration - The Problem: Clients request keys that do not exist in either the cache or the database (e.g., searching for a non-existent user ID).

*Applies **database-indexing** to the decision above.*

```architecture

  "version": 1,
  "title": "Caching Gotchas and Mitigation - Storage Topology",
  "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.",
  "view": "data-flow",
  "pattern": "cache-aside",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": [
    { "id": "compute", "label": "Application Workers", "tone": "blue" },
    { "id": "cache-tier", "label": "Volatile Memory Tier", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "storage-tier", "label": "Persistent Disk Tier", "tone": "green" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "worker", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Worker Process", "group": "compute" },
    { "id": "mem", "component": "redis", "label": "In-Memory Cache", "group": "cache-tier", "badge": "Hot Keys" },
    { "id": "primary", "component": "postgres", "label": "Primary Database", "group": "storage-tier", "badge": "Write Master" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "worker", "to": "mem", "kind": "read", "label": "Fast Read" },
    { "from": "worker", "to": "primary", "kind": "write", "label": "Transactional Commit" }
  ],
  "takeaway": {
    "title": "Storage Access Pattern",
    "body": "In-memory caching handles high-frequency read spikes, reserving disk transactions strictly for state modifications."
  }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** Cache Penetration - The Problem: Clients request keys that do not exist in either the cache or the database (e.g., searching for a non-existent user ID).

## Stage 4 — Write-Around: Keep One-Time Writes Out of the Cache

- Write-around sends writes directly to the database and invalidates any old cached value.
- The cache is populated only if a later read needs the record.
- It is useful for imports, audit events, large objects, and other data that is written once but may never become hot.
- Its cost is predictable: the first read after every write is a cache miss.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Its cost is predictable: the first read after every write is a cache miss.

## Stage 5 — Practical Cache-Aside with Stampede Protection

- ~~~ts async function getProduct(id: string) { const key = 'product:v3:' + id; const cached = await redis.get(key); if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached); // SET NX lets one request rebuild the key.
- Others briefly retry or serve stale data.
- const lockKey = key + ':lock'; const ownsLock = await redis.set(lockKey, requestId, { NX: true, PX: 3 000 }); if (!ownsLock) return retryWithJitter(() = getProduct(id), 40, 120); try { const product = await db.products.…
- ttlSeconds : 30 }); return product; } finally { // Production code should compare the lock token before deletion.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** ttlSeconds : 30 }); return product; } finally { // Production code should compare the lock token before deletion.

## Stage 6 — Capacity Planning and Observability

- Suppose an API serves 20,000 reads per second, the database safely handles 2,500, and the target cache hit ratio is 90%.
- The expected database read rate is 2,000 per second: within budget, but with little room for a stampede.
- At 80% hits the database receives 4,000 reads per second and is already overloaded.
- Capacity planning must test degraded hit ratios, not only the happy path.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Capacity planning must test degraded hit ratios, not only the happy path.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- - A cache reduces load only while its miss path remains controlled.
- - Pattern choice is primarily a consistency and failure-semantics decision.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: Selecting the Caching Pattern

Use this guide to choose the caching strategy for your system: - Use Cache-Aside if: - Your application is read-heavy and you want to cache data dynamically.

### Redis vs Memcached: Choose Capabilities, Not Brand Recognition

Choose Memcached when values are disposable blobs, operations are simple, and rebuilding the entire cache is acceptable.


## Failure and degraded modes

The source does not isolate a separate failure mode. Limits that matter for the scenario are called out in the stage decisions above.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: Machine Learning Fundamentals
seriesList.description: This series breaks down complex mathematical theories and algorithms into simple, intuitive explanations with practical examples, making AI accessible to everyone from beginners to aspiring data scientists.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
